sorular.soru: One LLM can translate, summarize and answer questions. Why can a single model do such different tasks?
secenekler: Each task has its own encoder, stored inside the model
Each task was taught with human labels during pretraining
Each task can be put as text going in and text coming out
Each task is picked by the temperature setting at the end
sorular.aciklama: Translation, summaries and answers all take text in and give text out, so one next-token model can do them all. Pretraining has no human labels for each task, because the next token in the text is the label.

sorular.soru: An LLM predicts only one next token at a time. How does it still write a long answer?
secenekler: It adds each chosen token to the context and predicts again
It predicts all the tokens at once and then sorts them in order
It finds a stored answer that fits the context and copies it
It plans the whole answer as one vector and then unpacks it
sorular.aciklama: Generation is a loop: the model picks a token, adds it to the context and predicts the next one. It can not choose all tokens at once, because each new token depends on the ones before it.

sorular.soru: A simple keyboard app guesses your next word from only the last two words you typed. Which case is hardest for it?
secenekler: The last two words appeared many times in its training text
The next word is long and made of several subword pieces
The sentence is short and uses only very common words
The right word depends on a word much earlier in the sentence
sorular.aciklama: A short window can not see words further back, so it misses links like a subject far from its verb. Word pairs seen many times are the easy case, because their counts are reliable.

sorular.soru: Many word sequences are rare or never seen, so their counts can not be trusted. What does a model need to fix this?
secenekler: A wider window that counts more of the previous words
A way to learn from similar words, beyond exact matches
A larger vocabulary that keeps more whole words as tokens
A higher temperature that samples rare words more often
sorular.aciklama: Counts only know exact matches, so the model needs learned vectors that let similar words share what they learn. A wider window makes the problem worse, because longer sequences are even rarer.

sorular.soru: A user types a new product name that never appeared in the training text. How can the model still read it?
secenekler: The model adds the new name to its vocabulary while it is running
The model skips the name and reads only the other words around it
The tokenizer splits it into smaller pieces from its vocabulary
The embedding table makes a fresh vector for the whole new name
sorular.aciklama: Subword tokenization breaks a new or rare word into known pieces, so a fixed vocabulary can still cover it. The vocabulary and the embedding table stay fixed after training, so no new entry is added at use time.

sorular.soru: Single letters can spell any word, so a letter tokenizer never meets an unknown word. Why do LLMs still prefer subword tokens?
secenekler: Letters can not be turned into token IDs or into embedding vectors
Letters make every text much longer, so it costs more to process
Letters would make the vocabulary far too large to keep in memory
Letters carry no meaning, so attention would have nothing to use
sorular.aciklama: A letter vocabulary is tiny, but every text becomes a very long sequence, and the model pays for each token. Subwords are a middle path: a fixed vocabulary that still covers rare words with fewer tokens.

sorular.soru: Token IDs are just numbers in a list. Why does the model turn each ID into a learned vector before using it?
secenekler: A vector keeps the exact spelling, so the token can be rebuilt
A vector stores the token's position, so order is no longer needed
A vector holds the context, so the token differs in each sentence
A vector can put tokens with similar uses close to each other
sorular.aciklama: An ID is only a label, but a learned vector can carry meaning, so similar tokens get similar vectors. The input vector is the same in every sentence, and only the later layers make it depend on context.

sorular.soru: A student says: 'An LLM is just Word2Vec with a bigger vocabulary.' What key idea does this miss?
secenekler: LLMs use layers that change each token's vector to fit its context
LLMs learn no vectors at all and work directly on raw letters
LLMs give each meaning of a word its own fixed vector in a table
LLMs learn their vectors from human labels and not from raw text
sorular.aciklama: Word2Vec gives one fixed vector per word, but LLM layers turn the lookup vector into one that fits the context. The LLM does not keep a fixed vector for each meaning, because the context decides the meaning.

sorular.soru: In 'Maria thanked Tom because he helped her', the model must link 'he' to 'Tom'. What lets it make this link?
secenekler: A static embedding, which gives 'he' the same vector in every sentence
Attention, which lets 'he' look back and focus on the token 'Tom'
An n-gram window, which links 'he' only to the word just before it
A causal mask, which hides all the words that come after 'he'
sorular.aciklama: Attention lets each token use information from the tokens that matter most, so 'he' can focus on 'Tom'. A static embedding is the same in every sentence, so it can not tell which person 'he' means.

sorular.soru: An RNN encoder must pack a whole long sentence into one hidden state before the decoder starts. What problem does this cause?
secenekler: The decoder can see the later words, so it copies them instead of learning
The vocabulary must grow with every new sentence, so memory runs out
Details from early words fade, because one vector must hold everything
Each word needs its own weights, so the model grows with the sentence
sorular.aciklama: One hidden state of fixed size must carry the whole sentence, so details from early words get weaker step by step. An RNN uses the same weights at every step, so the model does not grow with the sentence.

sorular.soru: A team needs three tools: a spam filter for emails, a translator and a chatbot. Which model families fit them best, in the same order?
secenekler: Encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only
Decoder-only, encoder-only, encoder-decoder
Encoder-decoder, decoder-only, encoder-only
Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder
sorular.aciklama: A spam filter must understand the whole email, which encoder-only models do well, and translation maps one sequence to another. A chatbot writes its reply left to right, which is the job of decoder-only models.

sorular.soru: A user pastes a long report into a model with a very long context window. What does the long window really give?
secenekler: Perfect memory, so every detail of the report will be used well
New training data, so the model's weights learn from the report
A larger vocabulary, so every rare word in the report is known
Room for more tokens, but no promise that each part is used well
sorular.aciklama: The context window is the most tokens the model can use at once, but longer context is not perfect memory. Text in the window does not change the weights, so the report does not become training data.

sorular.soru: The last layer of an LLM gives a raw score for each token, and some scores are negative. Why is softmax used next?
secenekler: It keeps the single highest score and drops all the others
It turns the scores into positive chances that add up to one
It changes the weights so that the best token scores higher
It adds randomness so that each run gives a different token
sorular.aciklama: Logits can be any real numbers, and softmax makes them positive and scales them so they sum to one. Keeping only the top token is greedy decoding, which is a separate choice made after softmax.

sorular.soru: A model often gives a wrong answer to one question. A user lowers the temperature to get better answers. Now the wrong answer comes every time. Why?
secenekler: Low temperature sharpens the chances, so the top answer wins more often
Low temperature flattens the chances, so more wrong answers are drawn
Low temperature retrains the weights toward the most common answer
Low temperature removes the rare tokens from the vocabulary for that run
sorular.aciklama: A low temperature sharpens the same distribution, so the top answer wins almost every time, even when it is wrong. Flattening is what a high temperature does, and no decoding setting changes the weights.

sorular.soru: Pretraining uses huge amounts of raw text and no human labels. Where do the training targets come from?
secenekler: From people who rank the model's answers, as in preference tuning
From the quality filter, which marks each text as good or bad
From the text itself, since each next token serves as the target
From grammar rules that tag the role of every word in the text
sorular.aciklama: This is self-supervised learning: the next token already in the text is the label, so any text can become training data. People rank answers only later, in preference tuning, and not during pretraining.

sorular.soru: A model saw very little code during pretraining. Now it is weak at writing code. Which idea explains this best?
secenekler: The tokenizer can not split code into tokens of any kind
Code needs an encoder-only model, not a decoder-only one
The context window is too short to hold a full code file
The mix of the training data shapes what the model can do
sorular.aciklama: The mix of the data strongly affects what a model can and can not do, so a skill that is rare in the data stays weak. Code can be split into tokens like any other text, so the tokenizer is not the problem.

sorular.soru: Team A says its model is larger because it has more parameters. Team B says its model is larger because it saw more tokens. What does this show?
secenekler: Scale has several parts, and each team grew a different part
Scale means parameters alone, so Team B is using the word wrongly
Parameters and tokens are one thing, just counted in two ways
Scale means GPU work alone, so neither team's claim is valid
sorular.aciklama: Scale is not one number: model size, training data and GPU work all count. Parameters are only one part, so training on more tokens is also a real kind of scale.

sorular.soru: After scaling up, a model reaches a lower loss. The team says it is now safe and always correct. What does the lower loss really show?
secenekler: More training data, since loss can only fall when the data grows
A lower temperature, since loss falls when decoding is sharper
Better next-token guesses, which do not prove truth or safety
Memorized tests, since a low loss means the model saw the answers
sorular.aciklama: Loss measures how well the model predicts the next token, but probability is not truth, so adaptation, testing and careful use are still needed. Loss can also fall with a bigger model or more GPU work, so more data is not the only way.

sorular.soru: A hospital wants a model that knows medical words and writing well. Which step fits this goal best?
secenekler: Preference tuning, where people rank the answers for style and safety
Continued pretraining on medical text, with the same next-token task
A higher temperature, so rare medical words are drawn more often
A new tokenizer alone, with no further training of the model
sorular.aciklama: Domain adaptation keeps the next-token task but trains on medical text, so the model learns its words and style. Preference tuning shapes how the model behaves with users, and it adds little medical knowledge.

sorular.soru: After pretraining, a model sometimes gives rude or harmful replies to users. Which step is meant to change this behavior?
secenekler: Continued pretraining on more web text, with the same next-token task
A lower temperature, which updates the weights to avoid harmful words
A larger model, which reaches a lower loss on the same web text
Instruction and preference tuning, which shape helpful, safe replies
sorular.aciklama: Instruction and preference tuning adapt the style, helpfulness and safety of a base model. More web text of the same kind would teach the same patterns again, harmful ones included.
